name: LT3045EDD#TRPBF
title: 20 V, 500 mA ultralow noise, ultrahigh PSRR linear regulator
summary: The LT3045 is a 500 mA low dropout linear regulator built as a precision 100 µA current reference driving a unity-gain voltage buffer, so one resistor from SET to ground sets any output from 0 V to 15 V from a 1.8 V to 20 V input. Noise is 0.8 µVRMS (10 Hz to 100 kHz) and PSRR is 76 dB at 1 MHz, both essentially independent of the output voltage, and parts can be paralleled for more current and less noise. It adds a programmable current limit with output current monitor, programmable power good, fast start-up, a precision enable/UVLO input, and reverse-battery, reverse-current, foldback current limit and thermal protection. It is stable with 10 µF of ceramic output capacitance and comes in a 10-lead 3 mm × 3 mm DFN and a 12-lead MSOP.
key_figures: 1.8 V to 20 V (2 V to 20 V over temperature)
0.8 µVRMS, 10 Hz to 100 kHz, CSET = 4.7 µF
76 dB at 1 MHz; 117 dB at 120 Hz

notes: All are lead-free. The grade letter (E, I, H, MP) sets the temperature range; a label on the shipping container carries the grade.
Some packages also come on 500-unit reels with the suffix #TRMPBF.

pins.name: IN
pins.function: Supply input. Needs a bypass capacitor at the pin; 4.7 µF is usually enough, and large load steps may call for more. A battery's impedance rises with frequency, so battery-fed designs need the capacitor too. The part withstands IN taken negative with respect to GND, OUTS and OUT: with a reversed input it behaves like a diode in series with the input, no reverse current flows and the load sees no negative voltage.

pins.name: EN/UV
pins.function: Enable and undervoltage lockout. Low puts the part in shutdown: the output turns off and quiescent current falls below 1 µA. Turn-on is typically at 1.24 V rising with 130 mV of hysteresis, so a divider from IN to GND sets an input UVLO level. The pin may be driven above the input voltage. Tie to IN when unused; do not leave it floating.

pins.name: PG
pins.function: Power good, open collector. Pulls low while PGFB is below 300 mV. Leave open when unused. Parasitic diode to GND: keep it no more than 0.3 V below GND.

pins.name: ILIM
pins.function: Current limit programming. A resistor to GND sets the limit (nominal scale 150 mA·kΩ); for accuracy Kelvin-connect it to the GND pin. The pin sources 1/500 of the output current, so its voltage (0 V to 300 mV) monitors the output current. Tie to GND when unused. Parasitic diode to GND: keep it no more than 0.3 V below GND.

pins.name: PGFB
pins.function: Power good feedback. PG goes high when PGFB rises above 300 mV, with 7 mV of falling hysteresis. A divider from OUT to PGFB to GND sets the power-good threshold at 0.3 V × (1 + RPG2/RPG1). PGFB also controls the fast start-up circuit. Tie to IN when neither power good nor fast start-up is used; where reverse input protection is also needed, connect it through a 1N4148 with the anode at IN and the cathode at PGFB. Parasitic diode to GND: keep it no more than 0.3 V below GND.

pins.name: SET
pins.function: Regulation set point, and the inverting input of the error amplifier. A precision 100 µA flows out of the pin into a resistor to GND, and VOUT = ISET × RSET, from 0 V to 15 V. A capacitor from SET to GND lowers noise and improves PSRR and transient response, at the cost of a longer start-up. Kelvin-connect the ground end of the SET resistor at the load for best load regulation. Parasitic diode to GND: keep it no more than 0.3 V below GND.

pins.name: GND
pins.function: Ground.

pins.name: OUTS
pins.function: Output sense: the non-inverting input of the error amplifier. Run it by its own Kelvin trace to COUT and the load; the ground ends of COUT and CSET should meet directly. Parasitic diode to GND: keep it no more than 0.3 V below GND.

pins.name: OUT
pins.function: Regulator output. Needs at least 10 µF of output capacitance with ESR below 20 mΩ and ESL below 2 nH for stability; more capacitance holds down the peaks of large load steps. Parasitic diode to GND: keep it no more than 0.3 V below GND.

pins.name: GND
pins.function: Exposed pad, an electrical connection to GND. Solder it to the PCB ground and tie it straight to the GND pin for electrical and thermal performance.

tables.title: Absolute maximum ratings
rows: Operating junction temperature range, E-grade and I-grade
notes: Note 1. Operating beyond these ratings can damage the part for good; staying at any one of them for long periods can shorten its life and reduce its reliability.
Note 7. SET and OUTS each have a clamp of diodes with two 25 Ω resistors in series. For transients shorter than 5 ms the clamp can conduct more than the rated current.

Note 9. Tests run with pulsed loads so that TJ is close to TA. LT3045E: production tested at 25 °C, performance guaranteed from 0 °C to 125 °C, and the -40 °C to 125 °C range assured by design, characterization and statistical process control correlation. LT3045I: guaranteed over -40 °C to 125 °C. LT3045H: production tested at a 150 °C operating junction temperature. LT3045MP: production tested and guaranteed over -55 °C to 150 °C. Operating life is shortened at high junction temperatures and is derated above 125 °C.
Note 10. ILIM, PG, PGFB, SET, OUTS and OUT each have a parasitic diode to GND inside the part. In a fault none of them may go more than 0.3 V below GND; in normal operation each stays above GND.
Note 14. The OUT-to-OUTS limit is guaranteed by design.
Note 15. The MP grade comes only in the DFN package.

notes: Note 2. The part operates only once the EN/UV threshold is met.

Note 3. The regulated output figures do not cover every pairing of input voltage and output current: the maximum junction temperature bounds them, and the internal current limit folds back once VIN - VOUT exceeds 12 V. Run at maximum output current with a reduced input range, or at maximum input voltage with a reduced output current range.
Note 4. OUTS connected straight to OUT.

Note 5. Dropout is the input-to-output voltage at which the output has fallen 1 % below its regulated value at the stated current; hard dropout, taken at VIN = VOUT(NOMINAL), is lower. Below 1.5 V of output, the minimum input voltage figure sets the dropout. On the DFN package the maximum dropout at high currents is not guaranteed, because Kelvin contact to the package pins is limited in production test.

Note 6. Tested with a current-source load and the input at VOUT(NOMINAL), so the part is in dropout: this is the worst case, and the GND current falls as the input voltage rises. GND pin current leaves out the SET and ILIM pin currents; quiescent current counts them.

Note 8. A capacitor across the SET resistor bypasses both the resistor's thermal noise and the reference current noise, leaving the error amplifier noise as the output noise. It also lengthens start-up.
Note 11. The scale factor applies while the internal back-up current limit is inactive. The internal limit folds back for VIN - VOUT above 12 V.
Note 12. The back-up internal current limit folds back above a 12 V input-to-output difference, and some output current is available at every differential.
Note 13. Outputs below 1 V need at least 10 µA of load to stay stable.

circuits.title: Typical application: 5 V in, 3 V out at 500 mA
circuits.description: A 5 V supply in, 3 V out at up to 500 mA. The 100 µA SET current flows in a 30.1 kΩ resistor to set the output, with 4.7 µF across it for low noise. 249 Ω on ILIM programs the current limit. A 402 kΩ / 49.9 kΩ divider from the output drives PGFB, and 200 kΩ pulls PG up to the input. EN/UV is tied to the input. The input capacitor is optional.

circuits.title: Figure 1. Basic adjustable regulator
circuits.description: 100 µA into 33.2 kΩ sets 3.32 V, and OUT and OUTS together follow it. The 0.47 µF across the SET resistor cuts noise. EN/UV and PGFB both go to the input, so the part is always on and power good and fast start-up are unused. ILIM is grounded, leaving only the internal current limit, and PG is left open.

circuits.title: Figure 3. COUT and CSET connections for best performance
circuits.description: OUTS is taken to the output capacitor by its own trace, and the ground ends of RSET and CSET run to the ground terminal of COUT, so the capacitor is connected by four terminals and trace impedance stays outside the feedback loop. EN/UV and PGFB tie to the input; ILIM goes to ground and PG is open.
notes: RSET and CSET return to the ground terminal of COUT, not to a general ground point.

circuits.title: Figure 7. Parallel devices
circuits.description: Two regulators share one SET node, so one 16.5 kΩ resistor carrying 2 × 100 µA sets 3.3 V for both, with 0.47 µF across it for noise. Each output reaches the common 3.3 V rail through a 20 mΩ ballast, a short length of PCB trace, which evens out the load between them for a 1 A total. Both inputs, enables and PGFB pins share the 5 V supply; ILIM goes to ground and PG is unused.

circuits.title: 12 V in, 3.3 V out with 0.8 µVRMS integrated noise
circuits.description: A 12 V supply in, 3.3 V out at 200 mA with 0.8 µVRMS of integrated noise. 33.2 kΩ with 4.7 µF across it sets the output. 750 Ω on ILIM programs the current limit. A 453 kΩ / 49.9 kΩ divider from the output drives PGFB, 200 kΩ pulls PG up to the input, and EN/UV is tied to the input.

circuits.title: Low noise CC/CV lab power supply
circuits.description: A variable SET resistor sets the output voltage, VOUT(MAX) = 100 µA × RSET, and a variable ILIM resistor sets the output current limit, IOUT(MAX) = 150 mA·kΩ / RIOUT, so the part runs as a constant-voltage, constant-current supply. 0.47 µF across RSET filters noise. EN/UV and PGFB go to the input; PG is open.

circuits.title: Ultralow noise current source for RF biasing
circuits.description: A 200 mA current source into RLOAD, up to 15 V, from a 1.8 V to 20 V input. The 2 kΩ SET resistor returns to the load end of the 1 Ω R1 instead of to ground, so the regulated quantity is the voltage across R1. Output current noise is 0.8 µVRMS / ROUT with ROUT = R1 + RLOAD; a larger R1, with RSET raised with it, lowers it. 4.7 µF bypasses SET to ground and 10 µF sits on OUT. EN/UV and PGFB go to the input; ILIM is grounded and PG is open.
notes: VOUT(MAX) 15 V, IOUT 200 mA.

circuits.title: Programming undervoltage lockout
circuits.description: REN2 (110 kΩ) and REN1 (49.9 kΩ) divide the input down to EN/UV: the 1.24 V rising threshold turns the regulator on at 4 V of input, VIN(UVLO)RISING = 1.24 V × (1 + 110k/49.9k), and the hysteresis turns it off at 3.4 V. 33.2 kΩ with 0.47 µF sets 3.3 V at up to 500 mA. PGFB is tied to the input, so power good and fast start-up are unused and PG is open; ILIM is grounded.

circuits.title: Ratiometric tracking
circuits.description: U1 makes 3.3 V from 33.2 kΩ and 0.1 µF on its SET pin. U2's SET resistor, 16.9 kΩ with 0.1 µF across it, returns to U1's output instead of to ground, so U2's 5 V output is stacked on the 3.3 V rail and tracks it. The 3.3 V output needs at least 200 µA of load. Both parts share a 5.5 V to 20 V input with EN/UV and PGFB tied to it; ILIM is grounded and PG is open on both.

circuits.title: Ultralow 1/f noise reference buffer
circuits.description: An LTC6655-5 reference drives the SET pin through 1 kΩ, with 4.7 µF and 49.9 kΩ from SET to ground and 10 µF at the reference output. The regulator delivers the 5 V reference at up to 500 mA. EN/UV and PGFB go to the 6 V input; ILIM is grounded and PG is open.
notes: LTC6655-5 pins: 1 and 2 to the input, 3, 4 and 5 to ground, 6 and 7 the reference output.

circuits.title: Paralleling multiple devices using ILIM (current monitor) to cancel ballast resistor drop
circuits.description: Two regulators share the SET node, bypassed by 1 µF and returned through 16.5 kΩ to a node that RCDC (5 Ω) takes to ground. Each ILIM pin, which carries 1/500 of its output current, also feeds that node through 287 Ω; RCDC cancels the drop across the 20 mΩ ballast resistors. RILIM = 150 mA·kΩ / ILIM - RCDC × N gives 287 Ω for a 500 mA limit per regulator, and RCDC = RBALLAST × 500 / N gives 5 Ω, with N the number of parts in parallel. Output 3.3 V at up to 1 A; EN/UV and PGFB tie to the 5 V input and PG is unused.

circuits.title: Paralleling multiple LT3045s for 2 A output current
circuits.description: Four regulators share one SET node: 8.25 kΩ carrying 4 × 100 µA sets 3.3 V, with 4.7 µF across it. Each output feeds the common rail through its own 20 mΩ ballast and 10 µF, for 2 A in total with 300 mV of dropout. Output noise falls by the square root of the number of parts, 0.8 µVRMS / √4 = 0.4 µVRMS. U1 alone carries the power-good divider (453 kΩ / 49.9 kΩ from the rail) and a 200 kΩ PG pull-up to the input; the other three have PGFB tied to the input and PG open. All ILIM pins are grounded.

circuits.title: Low noise Wheatstone bridge power supply
circuits.description: The regulator supplies 3.3 V at up to 500 mA to a four-resistor bridge. With the LT3045's 0.8 µVRMS, the noise at VBRIDGE is 8 nVRMS with 1 % resistors (40 dB bridge PSRR) and 42.5 nVRMS with 5 % (26 dB). 33.2 kΩ with 4.7 µF sets the output, the 453 kΩ / 49.9 kΩ divider drives PGFB and 200 kΩ pulls PG up to the 5 V input; ILIM is grounded.
notes: VOUT 3.3 V, IOUT(MAX) 500 mA.

circuits.title: PGFB disabled without reverse input protection
circuits.description: PGFB tied straight to the input turns off both power good and fast start-up; EN/UV is also tied to the input. RSET with 0.47 µF across it sets the output. ILIM is grounded and PG is open.

circuits.title: PGFB disabled with reverse input protection
circuits.description: Power good and fast start-up disabled with reverse input protection: PGFB is fed from the input through a 1N4148, anode at the input. EN/UV goes to the input, RSET with 0.47 µF sets the output, ILIM is grounded and PG is open.

circuits.title: Parallel devices
circuits.description: Two regulators share one SET node, so one 16.5 kΩ resistor carrying 2 × 100 µA sets 3.3 V for both, with 0.47 µF across it for noise. Each output reaches the common 3.3 V rail through a 20 mΩ ballast, a short length of PCB trace, which evens out the load between them for a 1 A total. Both inputs, enables and PGFB pins share the 5 V supply; ILIM goes to ground and PG is unused.

equations.name: Output voltage
equations.note: Range 0 V to 15 V; the error amplifier runs at unity gain whatever the output.

equations.name: Power-good threshold
equations.expr: VOUT(PG_THRESHOLD) = 0.3 V × (1 + RPG2 / RPG1) + IPGFB × RPG2
equations.note: The IPGFB term is negligible when RPG1 is below 30 kΩ.

operation.text: A precision 100 µA current source feeds the SET pin, which is also the inverting input of a rail-to-rail error amplifier; a resistor from SET to ground turns the current into the reference voltage. The amplifier works as a unity-gain buffer driving the output, with OUTS as its non-inverting input. Because the gain never changes, loop gain, bandwidth, noise, PSRR and transient response are the same at every output voltage, and load regulation is specified in hundreds of microvolts rather than as a percentage.

The output runs from 0 V (a 0 Ω SET resistor) up to VIN less the dropout, at most 15 V. A PNP input pair works from 0 V to 0.6 V of output and an NPN pair above 1.3 V, with a smooth hand-over between 0.6 V and 1.3 V. The NPN pair gives the best overall figures; offset, SET current, noise and PSRR for each range are in the electrical characteristics.

With a zero-TC current source the SET resistor's tolerance tends to limit accuracy, so it should be a precision part. Any leakage into or out of SET shifts the output: 100 nA is a 0.1 % reference error. High-grade insulation (Teflon, Kel-F), cleaning off flux and, in humid conditions, a surface coating help. A guard ring round SET at nearly its own potential, ideally driven from OUT and on both sides of the board, cuts board leakage; how much depends on its width.

operation.topic: SET pin noise pickup and external drive
operation.text: SET is a high impedance node and can pick up interference, most noticeably with the minimum output capacitor at heavy load; 10 nF from SET to ground cures this. SET may instead be driven by a voltage source able to sink 100 µA, such as a precision reference, which removes the reference current and SET resistor errors.

OUTS gives a Kelvin sense of the output and the ground end of the SET resistor gives a Kelvin sense of the load ground. The loop bandwidth is about 1 MHz, close to the roughly 1.6 MHz self-resonance of a 10 µF 1206 ceramic capacitor, so ESR and ESL outside the loop must be kept small: run OUTS straight to COUT, join the ground ends of CSET and COUT directly, and keep the CIN and COUT grounds close. The part does not oscillate without this layout, but phase margin, noise and PSRR can suffer.

Stability needs at least 10 µF of low ESR, low ESL ceramic output capacitance, with ESR under 20 mΩ and ESL under 2 nH. Going larger barely improves noise or PSRR because the regulator bandwidth falls as capacitance rises, but it does reduce the peak excursion in a load transient. Decoupling capacitors on the powered circuits add to the effective output capacitance.

Z5U and Y5V capacitors pack high capacitance into small cases but lose much of it with voltage and temperature; a 16 V 10 µF Y5V part on a 5 V rail can fall to 1 µF to 2 µF over temperature. X5R and X7R are more stable and suit the part, X7R being better over temperature and X5R cheaper and available in larger values. Even these lose capacitance under DC bias, less so in larger cases, so the capacitance at the working voltage should be checked. Murata GJ8 series parts are recommended for their small voltage coefficient.

Ceramic capacitors can turn vibration or thermal stress into voltage. On the output and input this adds negligible noise because the output impedance is very low and PSRR is very high, but a ceramic SET capacitor can put hundreds of microvolts peak-to-peak on the output. Since SET tolerates high ESR and ESL, a non-piezoelectric type (tantalum, electrolytic or film) suits that position, though electrolytics have high 1/f noise; a surface-mount part is recommended.

4.7 µF of low ESR ceramic at IN is the minimum for stability. Long supply wires with a small input capacitor and a heavy load form an LC tank that can oscillate; add about 1 µF per 6 inches of wire on top of the 4.7 µF, more output capacitance (less effective than input capacitance), 0.1 Ω to 0.5 Ω of series resistance at the cost of dropout, or a tantalum or electrolytic part of higher ESR in parallel with the 4.7 µF ceramic. A battery mounted close to the part needs only the 4.7 µF.

Wire self-inductance grows with length and only weakly falls with diameter: a 2-AWG wire 0.26 inch across has about half the inductance of a 30-AWG wire 0.01 inch across, and one foot of 30-AWG wire is about 465 nH. Splitting the current over two parallel wires spaced a few inches apart cuts inductance by up to 50 %, less when they are close. Running the supply and return wires close together works better: two 30-AWG wires 0.02 inch apart have about one fifth the inductance of a single wire.

When the part post-regulates a switching converter, switching-frequency current in the input capacitor near the part creates a magnetic field that couples into the output; depending on the layout this can cost over 30 dB of PSRR at 1 MHz, and the loss remains even with the regulator removed. The input capacitor can be left off if the converter's output capacitor is more than an inch away, but with no input capacitor and the converter more than a couple of inches away the input will oscillate at the parasitic LC frequency. The LT3045 demo board layout uses magnetic field cancellation to keep the input capacitor without the PSRR loss.

PSRR removes a switcher's ripple, typically 100 kHz to 4 MHz, but the spikes from its switch transitions, in the hundreds of MHz, are beyond the regulator's bandwidth and pass almost straight through; the output capacitor's ESL limits how much it absorbs. A ferrite bead, or the inductance of a short PCB trace (about 0.5 inch) between the switcher output and the regulator input, forms an LC filter against them.

There is no voltage reference: the 100 µA reference current has a noise of 20 pA/√Hz (6 nARMS from 10 Hz to 100 kHz), which multiplied by RSET and summed with the resistor's own noise and the amplifier's gives the output noise. With a capacitor bypassing RSET the output noise is just the error amplifier's, typically 2 nV/√Hz from 10 kHz to 1 MHz and 0.8 µVRMS from 10 Hz to 100 kHz with 4.7 µF, independent of the output voltage. Paralleling N parts lowers it by √N.

A SET bypass capacitor also improves PSRR and transient response, and it soft-starts the output and limits inrush, the ramp to 90 % taking about 2.3 × RSET × CSET. Leakage in this capacitor degrades DC regulation (100 nA is a 0.1 % error), so a good low-leakage ceramic is recommended. The protection clamp sets a maximum CSET of 22 µF.

For low 1/f noise below 100 Hz a large SET capacitor, up to 22 µF, is needed, which would make start-up slow. While PGFB is below 300 mV the SET current is raised to about 2 mA, unless the part is in current limit, dropout or thermal shutdown or the input is below its minimum. Tying PGFB to IN, or to OUT for outputs above 300 mV, disables fast start-up and power good together. Both are disabled for outputs below 300 mV.

EN/UV puts the part into micropower shutdown. Its turn-on threshold is an accurate 1.24 V with 130 mV of hysteresis, so a divider from the input sets a precise undervoltage lockout; the pin current at the threshold enters the divider equation but can be ignored with REN1 below 100 kΩ. Tie EN/UV to IN when unused.

PG is an open collector that goes high impedance once PGFB rises above 300 mV. The comparator has 7 mV of hysteresis and 5 µs of deglitching. The PGFB pin current can be ignored with RPG1 below 30 kΩ. Leave PG open when unused.

ILIM trips at 300 mV. Its resistor to GND therefore fixes how much current ILIM may source, and through it the output current limit, at 150 mA·kΩ divided by the resistance. Kelvin-connect the resistor to the GND pin. Above 12 V of input-to-output difference the internal foldback lowers the internal limit, which can override the programmed one to keep the part in its safe operating area. ILIM carries 1/500 of the output current and can serve as a 0 V to 300 mV current monitor. Tie ILIM to GND when neither the limit nor the monitor is used.

After a step from full load to light or no load the output overshoots before the pass device turns off, and with little load the output capacitor would discharge slowly. When OUTS is above SET a current sink, typically about 4 mA, pulls the output down, and it stays on until whatever holds OUTS high lets go. It is disabled for inputs below 2.5 V or outputs below 1.5 V.

Connect the SET pins of every part to one node and the IN pins to one supply, and join the OUT pins through small ballast resistors made of PCB trace (Table 2). The worst-case offset of 2 mV per part keeps the ballast small: two parts each with 20 mΩ share within 20 % at full load, and the ballasts add only 10 mV of drop at 1 A, 0.3 % of a 3.3 V output. More than two parts can be paralleled for more current and less noise, and paralleling spreads the heat; at high input-to-output voltage a series input resistor, or one in parallel with the part, also spreads heat. Each OUTS ties directly to its own output capacitor.
High bandwidth and high PSRR call for careful layout; the recommended DFN layout is that of the DC2491A demo board.

Thermal shutdown is nominally 165 °C with about 8 °C of hysteresis. For continuous operation keep the junction at or below 125 °C (E and I grades) or 150 °C (H and MP grades). The exposed pad on both packages connects the die attach to the PCB, which serves as the heat sink; copper area, copper weight, layout and thermal vias set the thermal resistance (Tables 3 and 4; JESD51-7 and JESD51-12 describe the test boards).

Safe operating area protection cuts the current limit as the input-to-output difference rises above 12 V, but some output current is always available. At power-up the output follows the input, keeping the difference low so the part can start into heavy loads. With a high input, a low output and a heavy load, as after a short is removed or when EN/UV is raised with the input already present, the load line can cross the current-limit curve twice, giving two stable points; the input may then need to be cycled to zero and back for the output to recover.

Current limit and thermal overload protection guard against output faults. A clamp between SET and OUTS protects the error amplifier and carries up to 20 mA DC, so a voltage source driving SET must be limited to 20 mA. IN withstands -20 V without input current and without a negative output. With a backup battery holding the output up while the input is grounded, at an intermediate voltage or open, no current flows back to the input, but unless SET is floating current can flow to ground through the SET resistor (via the OUTS-to-SET clamp) and up to 15 mA through the overshoot recovery circuit; a Schottky diode from OUTS (anode) to SET greatly reduces the latter.
